questions.topic: Unit IX: Biotechnology and its Applications
questions.question: According to NCERT, about how many recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use the world over, and how many of these are presently marketed in India?
options: A) About 12 approved; 30 marketed in India
B) About 30 approved; 12 marketed in India
C) About 300 approved; 120 marketed in India
D) About 30 approved; none marketed in India
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) About 30 approved; 12 marketed in India
Why: NCERT states that at present, about 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use the world over, and in India, 12 of these are presently being marketed. Recombinant DNA technology allows mass production of safe and more effective therapeutic drugs that do not induce unwanted immunological responses.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the figures. (C) inflates both figures tenfold. (D) is wrong — 12 are marketed in India.
Key point: Human insulin is the best-known recombinant therapeutic.

questions.question:
Arrange the following in the order in which they appeared during human evolution, from earliest to latest:
(A) Homo erectus
(B) Australopithecines
(C) Neanderthal man
(D) Homo habilis
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: NCERT: about 2 mya, Australopithecines lived in East African grasslands (B); the first human-like being, Homo habilis, had a brain capacity of 650–800 cc (D); Homo erectus, about 1.5 mya, had a brain of around 900 cc (A); and Neanderthal man, with a brain of 1400 cc, lived in the near east and central Asia between 1,00,000 and 40,000 years ago (C).
Why not the others: (A) places H. erectus before H. habilis. (B) places H. habilis before the Australopithecines. (D) places Neanderthal man before H. erectus.
Key point: Brain capacity increased through the sequence.

questions.topic: Unit IX: Biotechnology and its Applications
questions.question: In the biolistics or gene gun method, which is suitable for plants, cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles coated with DNA. These particles are made of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Gold or tungsten
Why: NCERT states that in the biolistics or gene gun method, cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA. This method is suitable for plants.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not the metals used. Calcium ions are used for making bacterial cells competent, not as gene-gun particles.
Key point: Microinjection is used for animal cells; biolistics for plant cells.

questions.topic: Unit IX: Biotechnology and its Applications
questions.question: In discussing biopiracy, NCERT states that there are an estimated 200,000 varieties of rice in India alone, and that the number of documented varieties of basmati grown in India is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 27
Why: NCERT states that it is estimated that there are about 200,000 varieties of rice in India alone, and there are 27 documented varieties of basmati grown in India. Basmati is distinct for its unique aroma and flavour.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not the NCERT figure.
Key point: In 1997, an American company got patent rights on basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Biology and Human Welfare
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Drug)
(A) Morphine
(B) Heroin
(C) Cocaine
(D) Cannabinoids

List-II (Feature)
(I) Interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine
(II) A very effective sedative and painkiller, useful in patients who have undergone surgery
(III) Interact with receptors present principally in the brain; obtained from Cannabis sativa
(IV) Chemically diacetylmorphine; a depressant that slows down body functions
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: NCERT describes morphine as a very effective sedative and painkiller (II); heroin (smack) as diacetylmorphine, a depressant (IV); cocaine, from Erythroxylum coca, as interfering with the transport of dopamine (I); and cannabinoids as interacting with cannabinoid receptors present principally in the brain (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps morphine and heroin; (C) swaps heroin and cocaine; (D) swaps cocaine and cannabinoids.
Key point: Opioids bind to opioid receptors in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Biology and Human Welfare
questions.question: In AIDS, the person's immunity becomes so weak that they cannot protect themselves against infections. This is because HIV progressively decreases the number of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Helper T-lymphocytes
Why: NCERT explains that HIV enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates and produces progeny viruses, which attack other helper T-lymphocytes. This is repeated, leading to a progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes in the body of the infected person.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are not the main targets. (B) B-lymphocytes produce antibodies but are not the cells that HIV progressively destroys.
Key point: Macrophages act like an HIV factory; helper T cells are destroyed.

questions.topic: Unit IX: Biotechnology and its Applications
questions.question: NCERT lists several areas in which biotechnology has been applied. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: A) Mining of metal ores by blasting
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mining of metal ores by blasting
Why: NCERT states that biotechnology has given many useful products in the areas of therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops for agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment and energy production. Mining by blasting is not a biotechnological application.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are all listed by NCERT.
Key point: Biotechnology uses organisms or their parts to make useful products.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Biology and Human Welfare
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Microbe)
(A) Streptococcus
(B) Trichoderma polysporum
(C) Monascus purpureus
(D) Aspergillus niger

List-II (Product)
(I) Statins, used as blood-cholesterol-lowering agents
(II) Citric acid
(III) Streptokinase, used as a 'clot buster'
(IV) Cyclosporin A, used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ transplants
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: NCERT states that streptokinase, produced by Streptococcus, is used as a clot buster (III); cyclosporin A, produced by Trichoderma polysporum, is used as an immunosuppressive agent (IV); statins produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus are blood-cholesterol-lowering agents (I); and Aspergillus niger (a fungus) produces citric acid (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Trichoderma and Monascus; (B) swaps Streptococcus and Trichoderma; (D) swaps Monascus and Aspergillus.
Key point: Statins competitively inhibit the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cholesterol.

questions.sub_topic: Primary productivity — dependence and global figures
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about primary productivity:
(A) Primary productivity depends on the plant species inhabiting a particular area.
(B) It also depends on environmental factors, availability of nutrients and the photosynthetic capacity of plants.
(C) The annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter.
(D) Although oceans occupy about 70 per cent of the Earth's surface, they contribute the larger share of this, about 115 billion tons.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are NCERT statements about primary productivity.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — NCERT states that, despite occupying about 70 per cent of the surface, the productivity of the oceans is only 55 billion tons; the land produces the rest. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Primary productivity varies with the type of ecosystem.

questions.sub_topic: Parturition — hormone from the maternal pituitary
questions.question: Signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta induce mild uterine contractions called the foetal ejection reflex. This triggers the release of a hormone from the maternal pituitary that causes stronger uterine contractions. The hormone is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Oxytocin
Why: NCERT states that the foetal ejection reflex triggers the release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary. Oxytocin acts on the uterine muscle and causes stronger uterine contractions, which in turn stimulate further secretion of oxytocin, leading to the expulsion of the baby.
Why not the others: (D) Prolactin is linked with milk production. (B) Progesterone maintains pregnancy. (C) Relaxin is secreted by the ovary in the later phase of pregnancy.
Key point: Parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism.

questions.topic: Unit IX: Biotechnology and its Applications
questions.sub_topic: Breaking fungal cell walls to release DNA
questions.question: To release DNA from fungal cells for genetic engineering, the cells are treated with an enzyme that breaks down the fungal cell wall. This enzyme is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Chitinase
Why: NCERT states that the cells are treated with enzymes such as lysozyme (bacteria), cellulase (plant cells) and chitinase (fungus) to break the cell wall and release DNA along with other macromolecules.
Why not the others: (A) is used for bacteria. (B) is used for plant cells. (C) Ribonuclease removes RNA from the extract; it does not break cell walls.
Key point: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin.

questions.question: Morgan found 1.3 per cent recombination between the genes for white eye and yellow body, but 37.2 per cent between the genes for white eye and miniature wing in Drosophila. This means that:
options: A) White eye and yellow body genes are tightly linked
B) White eye and miniature wing genes are tightly linked
C) All three genes are located on different chromosomes
D) Recombination does not depend on the distance between genes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) White eye and yellow body genes are tightly linked
Why: NCERT explains that when genes are tightly linked, they show very low recombination; when loosely linked, they show higher recombination. The 1.3% value for white eye–yellow body shows tight linkage; the 37.2% value shows loose linkage.
Why not the others: (B) The 37.2% value shows loose linkage. (C) All of these genes are on the X chromosome. (D) Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequency as a measure of distance between genes to map them.
Key point: Low recombination → genes are close together.

questions.topic: Unit IX: Biotechnology and its Applications
questions.sub_topic: Three critical research areas of biotechnology
questions.question: NCERT identifies three critical research areas of biotechnology. One of them is:
options: A) Breeding livestock without any use of microbes
B) Designing new antibiotics by computer modelling alone
C) Mapping the location of all human genes on chromosomes
D) Developing downstream processing to purify the protein or compound
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Developing downstream processing to purify the protein or compound
Why: NCERT lists the three critical research areas of biotechnology as: (i) providing the best catalyst in the form of an improved organism, usually a microbe or pure enzyme; (ii) creating optimal conditions through engineering for a catalyst to act; and (iii) downstream processing technologies to purify the protein or organic compound.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not among the three areas NCERT names.
Key point: Catalyst → optimal conditions → purification.

questions.sub_topic: Grazing and detritus food chains — share of energy
questions.question: According to NCERT, the relative importance of the grazing food chain (GFC) and the detritus food chain (DFC) differs between ecosystems. Which statement is correct?
options: A) In all ecosystems, the GFC and the DFC carry equal shares of energy
B) The DFC carries most energy in aquatic ecosystems, and the GFC on land
C) Detritus food chains never occur in terrestrial ecosystems at all
D) The GFC is the major conduit in aquatic ecosystems; on land, the DFC carries more
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The GFC is the major conduit in aquatic ecosystems; on land, the DFC carries more
Why: NCERT states that in an aquatic ecosystem, the GFC is the major conduit for energy flow. In contrast, in a terrestrial ecosystem, a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain than through the GFC.
Why not the others: (A) The shares are not equal. (B) reverses the NCERT statement. (C) Detritus food chains are very important on land.
Key point: The DFC begins with dead organic matter and is made up of decomposers.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the effect of natural selection on a trait that shows a normal distribution in a population:
(A) In stabilising selection, more individuals acquire the mean character value.
(B) In directional selection, more individuals acquire a value other than the mean character value.
(C) In disruptive selection, more individuals acquire values at both peripheral ends of the distribution curve.
(D) Disruptive selection increases the number of individuals with the mean character value.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: NCERT describes these three effects of natural selection: stabilisation, where more individuals acquire the mean character value (A); directional change, where more individuals acquire a value other than the mean (B); and disruption, where more individuals acquire peripheral character values at both ends (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — disruptive selection REDUCES the frequency of the mean character value, favouring both extremes. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Stabilising → mean; directional → one end; disruptive → both ends.

questions.question: In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected, and tribal communities also protect sacred groves. In Meghalaya, sacred groves are found in the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Khasi and Jaintia Hills
Why: NCERT lists sacred groves in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh.
Why not the others: (A) is in Rajasthan. (B) are in Madhya Pradesh. (C) is in Karnataka and Maharashtra.
Key point: In sacred groves, all the trees and wildlife are venerated and given total protection.

questions.question: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs 'sexual deceit' to get pollinated by a species of bee. This works because:
options: A) It provides bees with a safe place to lay their eggs
B) One petal of its flower resembles the female of the bee
C) Its flowers produce large amounts of nectar for bees
D) It releases a chemical that kills competing insects
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) One petal of its flower resembles the female of the bee
Why: NCERT explains that one petal of the Ophrys flower bears an uncanny resemblance to the female of the bee in size, colour and markings. The male bee is attracted to what it perceives as a female, 'pseudocopulates' with the flower, and is dusted with pollen, which it transfers to another flower.
Why not the others: (A) describes the fig–wasp relationship. (C) No nectar reward is involved in deceit. (D) is not described.
Key point: If the female bee's colour patterns change even slightly, the orchid must co-evolve to keep its resemblance.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Biology and Human Welfare
questions.question: Which of the following alcoholic beverages is produced by distillation of the fermented broth?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Rum
Why: NCERT states that depending on the type of raw material and the type of processing (with or without distillation), different types of alcoholic drinks are obtained. Wine and beer are produced without distillation, whereas whisky, brandy and rum are produced by distillation of the fermented broth.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are produced without distillation. (D) Toddy is a traditional drink made by fermenting sap from palms, not by distillation.
Key point: The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer's yeast) is used for fermentation.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Biology and Human Welfare
questions.sub_topic: Idli and dosa batter — bacterial fermentation
questions.question: The dough used for making idli and dosa is fermented by bacteria. Its puffed-up appearance is due to the production of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Carbon dioxide gas
Why: NCERT states that the dough used for making foods such as dosa and idli is also fermented by bacteria, and the puffed-up appearance of the dough is due to the production of CO₂ gas.
Why not the others: (B) Fermentation does not release oxygen. (C) Lactic acid sours the batter; it does not puff it up. (D) Methane is made by methanogens in anaerobic sludge and cattle rumen.
Key point: Baker's yeast puffs bread dough in the same way.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): David Tilman's long-term ecosystem experiments found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass.
Reason (R): Paul Ehrlich's 'rivet popper' hypothesis compares an ecosystem to an airplane, with the species as the rivets joining its parts together.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Both are NCERT statements. Tilman's outdoor plot experiments showed that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity and stability. Ehrlich's analogy describes why loss of species may threaten ecosystem function, but it is a hypothesis, not the explanation of Tilman's experimental result.
Why not the others: (A) The Reason does not explain the experimental observation. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Biodiversity is essential for ecosystem health.

questions.question: The scientist who united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Walter Sutton
Why: NCERT states that Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted that the behaviour of chromosomes was parallel to the behaviour of genes. Sutton united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
Why not the others: (B) Morgan provided experimental verification using Drosophila. (C) De Vries rediscovered Mendel's work and proposed the mutation theory. (D) Mendel did not know about chromosomes.
Key point: Genes are located on chromosomes.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II for the human female reproductive tract:

List-I (Part)
(A) Infundibulum
(B) Ampulla
(C) Isthmus
(D) Cervix

List-II (Feature)
(I) The last part of the oviduct, with a narrow lumen, that joins the uterus
(II) The funnel-shaped part closest to the ovary, with finger-like fimbriae
(III) Its canal, along with the vagina, forms the birth canal
(IV) The wider part of the oviduct that follows the infundibulum
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: NCERT describes the infundibulum as the funnel-shaped part closer to the ovary, with fimbriae that help in collecting the ovum after ovulation (II); the infundibulum leads to a wider part called the ampulla (IV); the last part, the isthmus, has a narrow lumen and joins the uterus (I); and the cavity of the cervix, the cervical canal, along with the vagina forms the birth canal (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps isthmus and cervix; (B) swaps infundibulum and ampulla; (C) swaps ampulla and isthmus.
Key point: Oviduct = infundibulum → ampulla → isthmus.

questions.topic: Unit IX: Biotechnology and its Applications
questions.sub_topic: Ideal gene therapy for ADA deficiency
questions.question: In gene therapy for ADA deficiency using lymphocytes, the patient needs periodic infusions of genetically engineered cells. According to NCERT, a permanent cure could be achieved by:
options: A) Giving the patient regular injections of the ADA enzyme
B) Transplanting bone marrow from an unrelated donor
C) Infusing the patient's own lymphocytes more often
D) Introducing the ADA gene into cells at early embryonic stages
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Introducing the ADA gene into cells at early embryonic stages
Why: NCERT explains that since engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusion. However, if the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could be a permanent cure.
Why not the others: (A) Enzyme replacement therapy is not fully curative. (B) Bone marrow transplantation is a treatment, but not the gene-therapy cure NCERT describes. (C) More frequent infusion is not permanent.
Key point: The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following is a copper-releasing intra-uterine device (IUD)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Multiload 375
Why: NCERT lists CuT, Cu7 and Multiload 375 as copper-releasing IUDs. The Cu ions released suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms.
Why not the others: (A) Lippes loop is a non-medicated IUD. (B) LNG-20 is a hormone-releasing IUD. (D) Saheli is an oral pill, not an IUD.
Key point: IUDs are inserted by doctors or expert nurses in the uterus through the vagina.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about medical termination of pregnancy (MTP), as given by NCERT:
(A) Nearly 45 to 50 million MTPs are performed in a year all over the world, accounting for about one-fifth of all conceived pregnancies.
(B) MTPs are considered relatively safe during the first trimester, i.e., up to 12 weeks of pregnancy.
(C) Second-trimester abortions are much more risky.
(D) MTP is legally permitted in India for selecting the sex of the child.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are NCERT statements about MTP.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — NCERT warns that misuse of amniocentesis and MTP for female foeticide (sex selection) is illegal and dangerous. Options (A) and (B) include it, and (C) leaves out the true statement (B).
Key point: MTP is allowed under the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017, under specified conditions only.

questions.sub_topic: Why not every copulation leads to fertilisation
questions.question: According to NCERT, all copulations do not lead to fertilisation and pregnancy, because fertilisation can occur only if:
options: A) The ovum and sperms are transported together to the ampullary region
B) The sperms reach the uterus within the first 12 hours of the cycle
C) The ovum is released directly into the uterine cavity
D) More than one sperm enters the ovum at the same time
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The ovum and sperms are transported together to the ampullary region
Why: NCERT states that fertilisation takes place in the ampullary region of the fallopian tube, and it can occur only if the ovum and sperms are transported simultaneously to the ampullary region. This is the reason why not all copulations lead to fertilisation and pregnancy.
Why not the others: (B) Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla, not the uterus. (C) The ovum is released into the oviduct region. (D) Entry of additional sperms is blocked by the zona pellucida.
Key point: Ampulla = site of fertilisation.

questions.question:
NCERT records two remarkable cases of old seeds that germinated:

Seed | Where found | Approximate age when it germinated
Lupinus arcticus | Arctic tundra | 10,000 years
Phoenix dactylifera (date palm) | King Herod's palace, near the Dead Sea | 2,000 years

These records show that:
options: A) Seeds of all plants germinate within a year of dispersal
B) Seeds can stay viable for very long periods in a dormant state
C) Only seeds of desert plants can survive for long periods
D) Old seeds germinate only if fertilised for a second time
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Seeds can stay viable for very long periods in a dormant state
Why: NCERT notes that the viability of seeds after dispersal varies — in a few species seeds lose viability within a few months, while seeds of a large number of species live for several years; some seeds remain alive for hundreds of years. The oldest records are a Lupinus arcticus seed from the Arctic tundra that germinated after about 10,000 years of dormancy, and a 2000-year-old date palm seed.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts the records. (C) Lupinus arcticus is from the Arctic tundra, not a desert. (D) Seeds are not fertilised again.
Key point: Dormancy lets seeds wait for favourable conditions.

questions.question: Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults are barrier methods of contraception. Which statement about them is correct?
options: A) They are worn by males over the penis during coitus
B) They release copper ions that reduce sperm motility
C) They are hormonal implants placed under the skin
D) They are made of rubber, cover the cervix, and are reusable
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) They are made of rubber, cover the cervix, and are reusable
Why: NCERT states that diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults are barriers made of rubber that are inserted into the female reproductive tract to cover the cervix during coitus. They prevent conception by blocking the entry of sperms through the cervix, and they are reusable. Spermicidal creams, jellies and foams are usually used with them to increase their efficiency.
Why not the others: (A) describes condoms. (B) describes copper-releasing IUDs. (C) describes implants.
Key point: Barrier methods prevent the physical meeting of sperm and ovum.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Biology and Human Welfare
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the life cycle of Plasmodium:
(A) Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.
(B) The parasites multiply initially within the liver cells and then attack the red blood cells, resulting in their rupture.
(C) The rupture of RBCs releases haemozoin, which causes chill and high fever recurring every three to four days.
(D) Fertilisation and development of the parasite take place in the red blood cells of humans.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are NCERT descriptions of the human stages of the malarial parasite.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the sexual stages (gametocytes) develop in the RBCs, but fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's intestine, and the sporozoites are stored in its salivary glands. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Plasmodium needs two hosts — humans and the female Anopheles mosquito.

questions.question: Failure of cytokinesis after the telophase stage of cell division results in an increase in a whole set of chromosomes in an organism. This phenomenon, often seen in plants, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Polyploidy
Why: NCERT defines polyploidy as an increase in a whole set of chromosomes resulting from failure of cytokinesis after telophase, a condition often seen in plants.
Why not the others: (A) Aneuploidy is the gain or loss of one or a few chromosomes, due to failure of segregation of chromatids. (B) and (C) are types of aneuploidy (2n + 1 and 2n − 1).
Key point: Whole sets → polyploidy; single chromosomes → aneuploidy.

questions.sub_topic: Modern humans — timeline of cave art and agriculture
questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs an event in human history with its approximate time, as given by NCERT?
options: A) Pre-historic cave art developed — about 18,000 years ago
B) Agriculture began — about 1,00,000 years ago
C) Homo erectus appeared — about 15 million years ago
D) Dryopithecus was walking about — about 2 million years ago
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Pre-historic cave art developed — about 18,000 years ago
Why: NCERT states that pre-historic cave art developed about 18,000 years ago. Agriculture came around 10,000 years back, and human settlements started.
Why not the others: (B) Agriculture began about 10,000 years ago. (C) Homo erectus appeared about 1.5 million years ago. (D) Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus existed about 15 million years ago.
Key point: Modern Homo sapiens arose during the ice age between 75,000 and 10,000 years ago.

questions.sub_topic: Path of sperms through the male ducts
questions.question:
Arrange the following parts of the male reproductive system in the order in which sperms pass through them, starting from the seminiferous tubules:
(A) Vasa efferentia
(B) Rete testis
(C) Epididymis
(D) Vas deferens
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (A), (C), (D)
Why: NCERT states that the seminiferous tubules of the testis open into the vasa efferentia through the rete testis. The vasa efferentia leave the testis and open into the epididymis, which leads to the vas deferens; this ascends to the abdomen and loops over the urinary bladder, then joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to open into the urethra as the ejaculatory duct.
Why not the others: (A) places the vasa efferentia before the rete testis. (B) places the vas deferens before the epididymis. (D) places the epididymis before the vasa efferentia.
Key point: Tubules → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Biology and Human Welfare
questions.question: Amoebic dysentery (amoebiasis), in which houseflies act as mechanical carriers, is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Entamoeba histolytica
Why: NCERT states that Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite in the large intestine of humans that causes amoebiasis. Symptoms include constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, and stools with excess mucous and blood clots. Houseflies act as mechanical carriers, transmitting the parasite from faeces of infected persons to food.
Why not the others: (A) causes ascariasis. (C) causes typhoid. (D) causes malaria.
Key point: Contaminated food and water are the main source of infection.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In many flowering plants with bisexual flowers, pollen falling on the stigma of the same flower fails to bring about seed set.
Reason (R): Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen from fertilising the ovules, by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: NCERT describes self-incompatibility as a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil. This is exactly why self-pollen fails to give seed set.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason directly explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Self-incompatibility is one of the devices that discourage self-pollination and encourage cross-pollination.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Item)
(A) Species recorded by the IUCN (2004)
(B) Global species estimate by Robert May
(C) India's share of the world's land area
(D) India's share of global species diversity

List-II (Value)
(I) About 2.4 per cent
(II) Slightly more than 1.5 million
(III) About 8.1 per cent
(IV) About 7 million
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: NCERT states that the IUCN (2004) records slightly more than 1.5 million described species (II); Robert May places the global species diversity at about 7 million (IV); India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area (I), yet its share of the global species diversity is about 8.1 per cent (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the two global figures; (C) swaps India's two shares; (D) swaps May's estimate and India's land area.
Key point: India is one of the 12 mega-diversity countries of the world.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the seven pairs of contrasting traits that Mendel studied in garden pea?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Leaf size
Why: Mendel's seven characters were stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape and seed colour. Leaf size was not one of them.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are among the seven characters.
Key point: Mendel selected 14 true-breeding pea varieties as pairs that differed in one character.

questions.sub_topic: Intrinsic rate r — human population in India
questions.question: NCERT gives the value of the intrinsic rate of natural increase (r) for the human population in India in 1981 as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.0205
Why: NCERT states that the r value for the human population in India in 1981 was 0.0205.
Why not the others: (A) 0.015 is the r value for the Norway rat. (B) 0.12 is for the flour beetle. (D) is ten times the NCERT value.
Key point: r depends on birth rate and death rate; it is used in dN/dt = rN.

questions.question: In most plants the fruit develops only from the ovary. In some species, however, the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation, giving a 'false fruit'. An example is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Apple
Why: NCERT states that in a few species such as apple, strawberry and cashew, the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation; such fruits are called false fruits. Most fruits develop only from the ovary and are called true fruits.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are true fruits formed from the ovary. (C) Banana is a parthenocarpic fruit.
Key point: True fruit = ovary only; false fruit = ovary + thalamus.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Biology and Human Welfare
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Allergy is the exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens present in the environment.
Reason (R): The antibodies produced in response to allergens are of the IgG type.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
Why: The Assertion is NCERT's definition of allergy; the substances to which such a response is produced are called allergens (mites in dust, pollens, animal dander).
Why not the others: The Reason is false — NCERT states that the antibodies produced to allergens are of the IgE type. Allergy is due to the release of chemicals like histamine and serotonin from the mast cells. So (A), (B) and (D) are wrong.
Key point: Allergy → IgE, mast cells, histamine; treated with anti-histamines, adrenalin and steroids.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II for seeds:

List-I (Term)
(A) Perisperm
(B) Testa
(C) Micropyle of the seed
(D) Non-albuminous seed

List-II (Description)
(I) The outer seed coat, formed from the integuments of the ovule
(II) A residual, persistent nucellus, as in black pepper and beet
(III) A seed with no residual endosperm, as in pea and groundnut
(IV) A small pore that lets oxygen and water into the seed during germination
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: NCERT states that in some seeds, such as black pepper and beet, remnants of the nucellus persist as perisperm (II); the integuments of the ovule harden as tough protective seed coats (I); the micropyle remains as a small pore in the seed coat that facilitates entry of oxygen and water during germination (IV); and non-albuminous seeds, such as pea and groundnut, have no residual endosperm (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps perisperm and testa; (C) swaps micropyle and non-albuminous seed; (D) swaps testa and micropyle.
Key point: Albuminous seeds (wheat, maize, castor) retain part of the endosperm.

questions.sub_topic: Unidirectional energy flow and the second law
questions.question: Ecosystems need a constant supply of energy to synthesise the molecules they require. NCERT explains this as follows:
options: A) Energy is recycled endlessly between producers and decomposers
B) Producers make their own energy and need no outside source
C) Energy flow obeys the second law; it is degraded at each step
D) Nutrients and energy flow in exactly the same cyclic manner
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Energy flow obeys the second law; it is degraded at each step
Why: NCERT states that ecosystems are not exempt from the second law of thermodynamics. They need a constant supply of energy to synthesise the molecules they require, to counteract the universal tendency toward increasing disorderliness. The flow of energy is unidirectional — from the sun to producers and then to consumers.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) Energy is not recycled; nutrients are. (B) Producers capture energy from sunlight.
Key point: Energy flows; nutrients cycle.

questions.question: The tiger census in national parks and tiger reserves is often based on:
options: B) Per cent cover of the area
C) Counting every tiger by sight
D) The biomass of trees in the area
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Pugmarks and faecal pellets
Why: NCERT states that the tiger census in our national parks and tiger reserves is often based on pugmarks and faecal pellets — an indirect measure of population size.
Why not the others: (B) Per cent cover or biomass is used for plants. (C) Counting each individual is not feasible for elusive animals. (D) Tree biomass does not measure tigers.
Key point: Relative densities often serve the purpose of population studies.

questions.question:
A cross between true-breeding red-flowered (RR) and white-flowered (rr) snapdragon plants gave pink-flowered F1 plants. On selfing the F1, the F2 counts were:

Phenotype | Number
Red | 52
Pink | 101
White | 49

The best interpretation of these data is:
options: A) A 3 : 1 ratio, showing that red is completely dominant
B) A 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio, showing that two genes are involved
C) A 1 : 1 ratio, showing that the F1 was crossed with a recessive
D) A 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, in which the phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the same
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, in which the phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the same
Given: 52 + 101 + 49 = 202 plants.
Step 1: 52 : 101 : 49 ≈ 1 : 2 : 1
Step 2: RR = red, Rr = pink, rr = white — each genotype has its own phenotype
Step 3: So the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio (incomplete dominance)
Common mistake: (A) would need only two phenotypes in 3 : 1. (B) needs four classes from a dihybrid. (C) needs two classes from a test cross.
Key point: In incomplete dominance, the F1 has a phenotype intermediate between the parents.

questions.question: E. coli grown for many generations in a medium with ¹⁵NH₄Cl is transferred to a medium with ¹⁴NH₄Cl. If replication is semi-conservative, what fraction of the DNA molecules will be hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) after three generations in the ¹⁴N medium?
options: D) All of them, with no light DNA
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1/4, the remaining 3/4 being light
Given: Start with 1 heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N) molecule; three generations in ¹⁴N.
Step 1: After 1 generation → 2 molecules, both hybrid
Step 2: After 2 generations → 4 molecules: 2 hybrid, 2 light
Step 3: After 3 generations → 8 molecules: 2 hybrid, 6 light → hybrid = 2/8 = 1/4
Common mistake: 1/2 (B) is the value after two generations (as NCERT describes for 40 minutes). 1/8 (C) counts only one hybrid molecule. All hybrid (D) is the first generation.
Key point: The two original heavy strands persist, always in two hybrid molecules.

questions.topic: Unit IX: Biotechnology and its Applications
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about selectable markers in cloning vectors:
(A) A selectable marker helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of transformants.
(B) Genes encoding resistance to antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin are useful selectable markers for E. coli.
(C) Normal E. coli cells carry resistance against all of these antibiotics.
(D) Inserting foreign DNA within the tetracycline resistance gene of pBR322 causes the recombinant cells to lose tetracycline resistance.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A) and (B) are NCERT statements about selectable markers. (D) is true — insertion inactivates the tetracycline resistance gene, so recombinants lose tetracycline resistance but keep ampicillin resistance.
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — NCERT states that normal E. coli cells do NOT carry resistance against any of these antibiotics, which is why these genes work as markers. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Transformation is the procedure by which DNA is introduced into a host bacterium.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A forensic laboratory receives a blood stain from a crime scene and blood samples from three suspects, X, Y and Z. DNA is isolated from each sample, digested with the same restriction enzyme, separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a nylon membrane and hybridised with a labelled VNTR probe. The positions of the bands on the autoradiogram are recorded below (fragment sizes in kilobase pairs, kb):

Sample | Bands (kb)
Crime-scene stain | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect X | 2.1, 3.9, 6.8, 10.5
Suspect Y | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect Z | 1.5, 4.5, 7.3, 9.2

Question: The laboratory can tell the samples apart because DNA fingerprinting identifies differences between individuals in:
options: A) The sequence of genes that code for proteins
B) The number of chromosomes in each cell
C) Specific regions of repetitive DNA sequences
D) The amount of RNA present in white blood cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Specific regions of repetitive DNA sequences
Why: NCERT states that DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in some specific regions in DNA sequence called repetitive DNA, because in these sequences a small stretch of DNA is repeated many times.
Why not the others: (A) About 99.9 per cent of bases are the same in all people, and coding regions are less variable. (B) Chromosome number is the same (46) in normal humans. (D) DNA, not RNA, is analysed.
Key point: Repetitive DNA shows high polymorphism.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A forensic laboratory receives a blood stain from a crime scene and blood samples from three suspects, X, Y and Z. DNA is isolated from each sample, digested with the same restriction enzyme, separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a nylon membrane and hybridised with a labelled VNTR probe. The positions of the bands on the autoradiogram are recorded below (fragment sizes in kilobase pairs, kb):

Sample | Bands (kb)
Crime-scene stain | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect X | 2.1, 3.9, 6.8, 10.5
Suspect Y | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect Z | 1.5, 4.5, 7.3, 9.2

Question: The VNTR probe used by the laboratory detects satellite DNA. Which of the following is a feature of satellite DNA?
options: A) It forms the bulk major peak in density gradient centrifugation
B) It forms small peaks and does not code for any proteins
C) It is found only in bacteria and never in humans
D) It codes for the histone proteins of the nucleosome
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It forms small peaks and does not code for any proteins
Why: NCERT states that repetitive DNA is separated from bulk genomic DNA as different peaks during density gradient centrifugation. The bulk DNA forms a major peak, and the other small peaks are called satellite DNA. These sequences normally do not code for any proteins, but they form a large portion of the human genome and show a high degree of polymorphism.
Why not the others: (A) describes bulk DNA. (C) Satellite DNA forms a large part of the human genome. (D) Satellite DNA is non-coding.
Key point: Satellite DNA → basis of DNA fingerprinting.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A forensic laboratory receives a blood stain from a crime scene and blood samples from three suspects, X, Y and Z. DNA is isolated from each sample, digested with the same restriction enzyme, separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a nylon membrane and hybridised with a labelled VNTR probe. The positions of the bands on the autoradiogram are recorded below (fragment sizes in kilobase pairs, kb):

Sample | Bands (kb)
Crime-scene stain | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect X | 2.1, 3.9, 6.8, 10.5
Suspect Y | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect Z | 1.5, 4.5, 7.3, 9.2

Question: After electrophoresis, the separated DNA fragments were transferred to a nylon membrane. This step of the technique is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Blotting
Why: NCERT lists the steps of DNA fingerprinting (Southern blot hybridisation): isolation of DNA; digestion by restriction endonucleases; separation of fragments by electrophoresis; transferring (blotting) the separated fragments to synthetic membranes such as nitrocellulose or nylon; hybridisation with a labelled VNTR probe; and detection by autoradiography.
Why not the others: (B) joins DNA fragments. (C) is removal of DNA bands from a gel. (D) is introduction of DNA into a host.
Key point: Blotting fixes the fragments in position for hybridisation.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A forensic laboratory receives a blood stain from a crime scene and blood samples from three suspects, X, Y and Z. DNA is isolated from each sample, digested with the same restriction enzyme, separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a nylon membrane and hybridised with a labelled VNTR probe. The positions of the bands on the autoradiogram are recorded below (fragment sizes in kilobase pairs, kb):

Sample | Bands (kb)
Crime-scene stain | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect X | 2.1, 3.9, 6.8, 10.5
Suspect Y | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect Z | 1.5, 4.5, 7.3, 9.2

Question: Based on the autoradiogram, which suspect's DNA profile matches the crime-scene stain?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Suspect Y
Given: Stain bands = 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2 kb.
Step 1: Suspect X shares 2.1 and 6.8 only
Step 2: Suspect Z shares 4.5 and 9.2 only
Step 3: Suspect Y has all four bands, and no extra ones → a match
Common mistake: Sharing some bands (A, B, C) is not a match; every band must correspond.
Key point: DNA from every tissue of a person (blood, hair, skin, bone, saliva, sperm) shows the same pattern.

questions.sub_topic: Why bands vary — VNTR copy number
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A forensic laboratory receives a blood stain from a crime scene and blood samples from three suspects, X, Y and Z. DNA is isolated from each sample, digested with the same restriction enzyme, separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a nylon membrane and hybridised with a labelled VNTR probe. The positions of the bands on the autoradiogram are recorded below (fragment sizes in kilobase pairs, kb):

Sample | Bands (kb)
Crime-scene stain | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect X | 2.1, 3.9, 6.8, 10.5
Suspect Y | 2.1, 4.5, 6.8, 9.2
Suspect Z | 1.5, 4.5, 7.3, 9.2

Question: Suspects X and Z each share two bands with the stain, but at different positions. Why do the VNTR bands of different people appear at different positions on the autoradiogram?
options: A) The restriction enzyme cuts each person's DNA at random places
B) Each person's DNA has a different number of nucleotide types
C) The copy number of the VNTR varies, so fragment sizes vary
D) Electrophoresis separates the DNA according to its charge only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The copy number of the VNTR varies, so fragment sizes vary
Why: NCERT explains that a VNTR belongs to a class of satellite DNA called mini-satellite. A small DNA sequence is arranged tandemly in many copy numbers, and the copy number varies from chromosome to chromosome in an individual and between individuals. The size of a VNTR varies from 0.1 to 20 kb, so the hybridised bands differ in size and position. Each person inherits these alleles from the parents, which is why relatives may share some bands.
Why not the others: (A) The same enzyme cuts at the same specific sites. (B) All human DNA has the same four nucleotides. (D) DNA fragments have similar charge per unit length; they separate by size through the sieving effect of the gel.
Key point: Variable copy number → variable fragment size → individual-specific pattern.
